title.en: How the Moon and the Stars Came to Be

region.en: Bukidnon highlands, northern Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Bukidnon tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨北部布基農高地（布基農故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bukidnon: 'How the Moon and the Stars Came to Be', eBook #12814

summary.en: In the times when the sky was close to the ground and looked like coral rock, a spinster went out to pound rice, hanging her beads and comb on the sky. Each swing of her pestle struck the sky, and when she raised it too hard the sky rose up so far that she lost her ornaments forever: the comb became the moon and the beads became the scattered stars.
summary.zh: 天低近地、狀如珊瑚岩之時，一位女子外出舂米，將項珠與木梳掛於天上。杵每起落皆擊天空；一次她將杵舉得過重，天空驟然高升，飾物永不可得——木梳化為月亮，珠串化為散落之星。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bukidnon narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Bukidnon communities. Etiological tale: the rising sky and the transformation of ornaments into celestial bodies.

passages.text: One day, in the times when the sky was close to the ground and looked like coral rock, a spinster went out to pound rice. Before she began her work she took off the beads from around her neck and the comb from her hair, and hung them on the sky. Then she began working, and each time she raised her pestle into the air it struck the sky. For some time she pounded the rice in this way, and then she raised the pestle so high that it struck the sky very hard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'How the Moon and the Stars Came to Be'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Immediately the sky began to rise, and it went up so far that she lost her ornaments. Never did they come down again, for the comb became the moon, and the beads became the stars that are scattered about the heavens. Thus the pounding of rice explains both why the sky is far above the world and why the moon and stars hang in it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'How the Moon and the Stars Came to Be'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Great Crab and the Flood (Bukidnon)

region.en: Bukidnon highlands, northern Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Bukidnon tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨北部布基農高地（布基農故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bukidnon: 'The Flood Story', eBook #12814

summary.en: A very big crab crawls into the sea and crowds the water out over all the earth, covering the land. A month earlier a wise man had warned the people to build a large raft; they bound three layers of trees together and fastened the raft with a long rattan cord to a pole in the earth. White water poured from the hills, the sea covered even the highest mountains, and all drowned except those on the raft, which the cord held near their old home when the waters sank — the only people left in the world.
summary.zh: 一隻巨蟹爬入海中，將海水擠出，漫覆大地。早在一個月前，智者已囑人建大木筏；他們以三層巨樹緊緊綁成筏，用長藤索繫於地上木柱。白水自山間傾瀉，海水淹沒至高峰；除筏上人畜外盡數溺亡。水退之後，因藤索未斷，木筏仍近故土——他們便是世上僅存的人類。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bukidnon narrators; presented as an archival record. Flood cluster: caused here by a giant crustacean displacing the sea — tagged world-serpent as an interpretive mapping (a vast creature whose movement unleashes the deluge), not a literal serpent.

passages.text: A long time ago there was a very big crab, and it crawled into the sea. As it went in, it crowded the water out so that the sea ran all over the earth and covered all the land. About one moon before this happened, a wise man had told the people that they must build a large raft. They did as he commanded and cut many large trees until they had enough to make three layers; these they bound tightly together, and when the raft was done they fastened it with a long rattan cord to a big pole in the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bukidnon 'The Flood Story'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon the floods came. White water poured out of the hills, and the sea rose and covered even the highest mountains. The people and animals on the raft were safe, but all the others drowned. When the waters went down and the raft was again on the ground, it was near their old home, for the rattan cord had held. But these were the only people left on the whole earth, and from them the world began again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bukidnon 'The Flood Story'; not verbatim.

region.en: Bukidnon highlands, northern Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Bukidnon tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨北部布基農高地（布基農故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bukidnon: 'Magbangal', eBook #12814

summary.en: The powerful hunter Magbangal goes alone to clear land for planting, and his ten bolos and hatchets sharpen themselves on the stone and cut the forest with no hands to guide them. His wife, spying on him, breaks the magic: Magbangal wakes, seizes a bolo, and cuts off one of his own arms. He ascends to become the constellation Magbangal — appearing when it is time to plant rice — while his wife goes into the water and becomes a fish.
summary.zh: 獵人馬格邦加獨自前往墾地，其十柄波洛刀與斧頭自行就石磨利、無人操縱而砍伐林木。妻子窺探之舉破了法術：馬格邦加驚醒，抓起一刀自斷一臂。他升天化為馬格邦加星宿——稻作播種之季由此星昭示——妻子則入水化魚。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bukidnon narrators; presented as an archival record. The constellation is an agricultural sign-calendar; oracle-divination tag is used for the celestial sign that regulates the planting season.

passages.text: Magbangal was a good hunter who often went to a certain hill and killed wild pigs for food. One night, as the planting season neared, he told his wife he would go to the hill alone the next day to clear the land, and she was not to come. She begged to accompany him, but he refused, and in the morning she cooked rice and fish for him to eat on his return. He gathered up his ten hatchets and bolos, a sharpening stone, and a bamboo tube for water, and set out for the hill, where he cut small trees to make a bench and sat down upon it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Magbangal'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Magbangal spoke to his weapons: "You bolos must sharpen yourselves on the stone," and the bolos went to the stone and were sharpened. "You hatchets must be sharpened," and they also sharpened themselves. "Now you bolos cut all the small brush under the trees, and you hatchets must cut the large trees." The weapons went to work, and from his bench Magbangal watched the land being cleared while he slept. His wife, weaving a skirt at home, heard the trees continually falling and thought her husband must have found many helpers; walking toward the field, she stopped behind a tree and saw him asleep, while bolos and hatchets cut the trees with no hands to guide them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Magbangal'; not verbatim.

passages.text: She marveled that Magbangal had never told her of his power. Suddenly he jumped up, seized a bolo, and cut off one of his own arms; waking, he sat up and said, "Someone must be looking at me, for one of my arms is cut off." Knowing his wife was the cause, he went home with her, saying, "Now I am going away. It is better for me to go to the sky where I can give the sign to the people when it is time to plant; and you must go to the water and become a fish." Soon after he went to the sky and became the constellation Magbangal, and ever since, when the people see these stars appear, they know it is time to plant their rice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Magbangal'; not verbatim.

region.en: Bukidnon highlands, northern Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Bukidnon tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨北部布基農高地（布基農故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bukidnon: 'How Children Became Monkeys', eBook #12814

summary.en: A mother takes her two children along to color cloth in a carabao mud hole. As she stirs the dye pot, scalding water splashes her hand and she jumps and cries out; the children's laughter changes them into monkeys, and the shell spoons they hold become their tails. Their nails are still black from the days when, as children, they helped their mother dye cloth.
summary.zh: 母親攜二孩至水牛打滾的泥塘染布。攪動染鍋時滾水濺起燙手，她跳起驚叫；孩童大笑之際化作猿猴，手中貝殼湯匙化為其尾。猿猴的指甲至今仍黑——因為他們做孩子時曾幫母親染布。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bukidnon narrators; presented as an archival record. Etiological tale of monkey tails and black nails.

passages.text: One day a mother took her two children with her when she went to color cloth. Not far from her home was a mud hole where the carabao liked to wallow, and to this hole she carried her cloth, some dye pots, and two shell spoons. After she had put the cloth into the mud to let it take up the dark color, she built a fire and set over it a pot containing water and the leaves used for dyeing, and sat down to wait for the water to boil while the children played near by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'How Children Became Monkeys'; not verbatim.

passages.text: By and by, when she went to stir the leaves with a shell spoon, some of the water splashed up and burned her hand, so that she jumped and cried out. This amused the children, and their laughter changed them into monkeys, and the spoons became their tails. The nails of the monkeys are still black, because while they were children they had helped their mother dye the cloth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'How Children Became Monkeys'; not verbatim.

title.en: Bulanawan and Aguio: The Twin Brothers' Battle
title.zh: 布拉納萬與阿圭歐：雙生兄弟之戰

region.en: Bukidnon highlands, northern Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Bukidnon tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨北部布基農高地（布基農故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bukidnon: 'Bulanawan and Aguio', eBook #12814

summary.en: Twins Bulanawan and Aguio are separated in infancy when a whirlwind carries Bulanawan away to a far land, where he grows into a great warrior. Years later Aguio arrives in that land and, not knowing his brother, tries to steal his brother's wife; the duel shakes the earth. Rival second brothers sense the tremor and join the battle, and the quaking grows until Langgona's father, the twins' grandfather, arrives and makes peace — revealing that the combatants were brothers and grandsons.
summary.zh: 雙生子布拉納萬與阿圭歐幼時被旋風拆散，布拉納萬被吹至遠方，長成大勇士。多年後阿圭歐遠遊至此，不知彼此為兄弟，欲奪其嫂；二人決鬥撼動大地。各自的結拜兄弟感得地動，趕來助戰，震動加劇，大地幾乎崩裂。最後朗戈納之父——雙生子祖父——前來止戈，眾人方知交戰者竟是兄弟與孫輩。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bukidnon narrators; presented as an archival record. Twins/duality cluster: twin brothers whose battle shakes the cosmos, resolved by an elder peacemaker.

passages.text: Langgona and his wife had twin boys named Bulanawan and Aguio. When they were about two years old the mother took Bulanawan with her to the field to pick cotton, and while she was gathering more a great wind suddenly arose which wound the cotton around the baby and carried him away. Far away to a distant land the wind took Bulanawan, and in that place he grew up; when he was a man he became a great warrior. Aguio, too, grew into a great warrior, and one day he journeyed to this distant land, not knowing that his brother was there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Bulanawan and Aguio'; not verbatim.

passages.text: That same day Bulanawan and his wife sat resting on a large flat rock by the seashore, and Bulanawan fell asleep. Aguio, walking along the shore in his war-dress, thought the woman very beautiful and determined to steal her. He asked for some of her husband's betel-nut to chew; when she refused, he went forward to fight her husband, not knowing they were brothers. When his wife awakened him, Bulanawan sprang up, seized her, and put her in the cuff of his sleeve before coming forth to fight. They fought until their weapons were broken and the earth trembled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Bulanawan and Aguio'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Far away, the rival brothers of the two combatants felt the earth tremble, and each, fearing his brother was in trouble, hastened to the scene — one from the mountains, one by boat across the sea. They arrived at the same time and joined the battle. The trembling increased so much that Langgona, father of the twins, sought out the spot and tried to make peace, but he only made matters worse, and they all began fighting him, until the earth was in danger of falling to pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Bulanawan and Aguio'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the father of Langgona came and settled the trouble, and when all were at peace again they discovered that Aguio and Bulanawan were brothers and the grandsons of the peacemaker. Thus the tale binds the great quake-makers of the Bukidnon past into one family, and the shaking earth becomes the sign of kindred turned against kindred without knowing it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Bulanawan and Aguio'; not verbatim.

title.en: Origin: Toglai and Toglibon and the First Tribes
title.zh: 起源：托格萊與托格利邦及諸族之始

region.en: Cibolan, Mt. Apo, Davao, Mindanao, Philippines
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨達沃阿波火山錫博蘭

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bagobo: 'Origin', eBook #12814

summary.en: The first couple Toglai and Toglibon live at Cibolan on Mt. Apo. After their eldest children depart across the waters — returning only as the Spaniards and Americans — a three-year drought dries every river, and the surviving children leave in pairs, each pair carrying some household thing from which a tribe takes its name: stones for the Magindanau, women's baskets for the Bilaan. Only a boy and girl too weak to travel remain; finding a single stalk of sugar-cane, they drink its water and survive, and their children are called Bagobo.
summary.zh: 初民夫婦托格萊與托格利邦居於阿波火山之錫博蘭。長子女渡水遠去，後裔即所謂西班牙人與美國人。其後三年大旱，河川盡涸；倖存子女兩兩離散，各攜一物——攜石者成馬京達瑙族，攜婦籃者成比拉蘭族，諸族之名皆源於所攜之物或所居之地。唯餘一對因飢渴過甚而無力遠行者，尋得一莖甘蔗飲汁度日；其子孫遂名巴戈博。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bagobo narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Bagobo communities. Ethnogenesis legend naming Bagobo, Bilaan, and Magindanau; the late-colonial framing (Spaniards and Americans) is retained as recorded, noting the tale's living tradition of adaptation.

passages.text: In the beginning there lived one man and one woman, Toglai and Toglibon. Their first children were a boy and a girl, and when they were old enough they went far away across the waters seeking a good place to live. Nothing more was heard of them until their children, the Spaniards and Americans, came back. After the first boy and girl left, other children were born to the couple, but they all remained at Cibolan on Mt. Apo with their parents, until Toglai and Toglibon died and became spirits.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bagobo 'Origin'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon after, a great drought came which lasted three years. All the waters dried up, so that there were no rivers and no plants could live. "Surely," said the people, "Manama is punishing us, and we must go elsewhere to find food and a place to dwell in." So they started out. Two went toward the sunset carrying stones from Cibolan River, and after a long journey they reached broad fields of cogon grass and abundance of water; their children still live there and are called Magindanau, because of the stones the couple carried when they left Cibolan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bagobo 'Origin'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Two children went to the south carrying women's baskets (baraan), and settled where they found a good spot; their descendants are called Baraan or Bilaan, because of the women's baskets. So two by two the children of the first couple left the land of their birth, and in each place a new people developed — thus all the tribes in the world received their names from things the people carried out of Cibolan, or from the places where they settled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bagobo 'Origin'; not verbatim.

passages.text: All the children left Mt. Apo save a boy and a girl whom hunger and thirst had made too weak to travel. One day, when they were about to die, the boy crawled out to the field to see if there was one living thing, and to his surprise he found a stalk of sugar-cane growing lustily. He eagerly cut it, and enough water came out to refresh him and his sister until the rains came. Because of this, their children are called Bagobo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bagobo 'Origin'; not verbatim.

title.en: Lumabet and the White Deer: The Ascent to the Sky

region.en: Cibolan, Mt. Apo, Davao, Mindanao, Philippines
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨達沃阿波火山錫博蘭

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bagobo: 'Lumabet', eBook #12814

summary.en: Lumabet, who could talk at one day old and worked wonders, chases a white deer around the world nine times, feeding himself by planting the skins of one banana and one camote each night. He has the people kill and revive his father eight times to prove his god-given power, then leads all who believe him through the moving, jaw-like sky to the world above — the sky keeping the last man as its agreed prize. His son follows on an arrow and a golden gun carried by white bees, while one homesick follower is lowered on a chain of karan leaves and becomes an owl.
summary.zh: 盧馬貝特生而一日能言，行諸奇事。他追白鹿環繞世界九匝，夜夜植蕉皮與薯皮為食。為證其神授之力，他八度命眾人殺其父並以頭帶復活之。其後他引信眾穿過開闔如口之天界，天得最後一人為酬；其子乘箭與金槍，由白蜂引路升天。而一名思鄉者被以卡蘭草鏈垂降，落地化為貓頭鷹。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bagobo narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Bagobo communities. Ascension cluster: a people-led migration to the sky at the horizon; resurrection tag covers the thrice-killed and revived father, an interpretive mapping.

passages.text: Soon after people were created on the earth there was born a child named Lumabet, who lived to be a very, very old man. He could talk when he was but one day old, and all his life he did wonderful things, until the people came to believe that he had been sent by Manama, the Great Spirit. As a young man he had a fine dog, and one day the dog scented a white deer. Lumabet and his companions pursued the swift deer but could not catch it; on and on they went until they had gone around the world, and one by one his companions dropped out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumabet'; not verbatim.

passages.text: All the time Lumabet had but one banana and one camote for food, but each night he planted the skins of these, and in the morning he found a banana tree with ripe fruit and a sweet potato large enough to eat. So he kept on until he had been around the world nine times, an old man with gray hair. At last he caught the deer, and he called all the people to a great feast. While they made merry, Lumabet told them to take a knife and kill his father. They were greatly surprised, but did as he commanded; when the old man was dead, Lumabet waved his headband over him and he came to life again. Eight times they killed the old man at Lumabet's command, and the eighth time he was small like a little boy, for each time they had cut off some of his flesh. They were certain Lumabet was a god.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumabet'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One morning some spirits came to talk with Lumabet, and after they had gone he called the people into his house. Though the house was small and the people many, all went in and it did not seem crowded. Then he told them he was going on a long journey: all who believed in his power could go with him, while those who remained behind would be changed into animals and buso. He started out with many following, and those who refused were immediately changed into animals and buso. He led the people across the ocean to the place where the earth and sky meet, and there the sky moved up and down like a man opening and closing his jaws. "Sky, you must go up," commanded Lumabet, but the sky would not obey until Lumabet promised it the last man who tried to pass. The sky opened, the people entered, and near the last it shut down so suddenly that it caught not only the last man but also the long knife of the man before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumabet'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On that same day Lumabet's son, out hunting, did not know his father had gone to the sky. Tired of the chase, he leaned an arrow against a baliti tree and sat on it; slowly it began to go down and carried him to his father's place, but he could find no people there — only a gun made of gold. White bees in the house said, "You must not weep, for we can take you to the sky where your father is," and they flew him up on the gun, reaching the sky in three days. Most of the followers were content in the sky, but one was unhappy, always looking down at the land below. The spirits made fun of him and wished to take out his intestines so he would be like them and never die, but he begged to go home. Finally Manama told them to allow it; they made a chain of the leaves of the karan grass, tied it to his legs, and let him down slowly head first — and when he reached the ground he was no longer a man but an owl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumabet'; not verbatim.

title.en: In the Beginning: The Four Beings on the Hat-Sized Island
title.zh: 太初：斗笠之島上的四神

region.en: Lake Sebu region, South Cotabato, Mindanao, Philippines (Bilaan homeland)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨南哥達巴托省賽布湖（比拉蘭人故地）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bilaan: 'In the Beginning', eBook #12814

summary.en: Four beings live on an island no larger than a hat with a single bird; the bird flies across the waters and returns with earth, rattan, and fruit. Melu, the greatest, shapes and beats the soil like a woman molding pots, making the earth, and plants the fruit seeds. The beings first try to make people out of wax, which melts; then out of dirt — but Melu's companion sets the noses upside down. While his back is turned, Melu seizes each nose and turns it right, hurrying so that his finger-press at the root of the nose remains on every human face.
summary.zh: 四神居於僅如斗笠大小之島，島上唯彼等與一鳥。鳥飛越水域銜回泥土、藤與果實。至大者梅盧如婦人製陶般捶塑泥土而成大地，並植果核，藤蔓果樹滋長。四神先以蠟造人，置火即融；改以泥土塑形——同伴卻把鼻子捏反。趁其轉身，梅盧逐個扳正鼻樑，倉促之間以指壓鼻根，人臉上那道指痕至今猶在。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bilaan narrators; presented as an archival record. Clay-humans cluster (wax fails, earth succeeds, noses reversed).

passages.text: In the beginning there were four beings, and they lived on an island no larger than a hat. On this island there were no trees or grass or any other living thing besides these four people and one bird. One day they sent the bird out across the waters to see what it could find, and when it returned it brought some earth, a piece of rattan, and some fruit. Melu, the greatest of the four, took the soil and shaped it and beat it with a paddle in the same manner in which a woman shapes pots of clay, and when he finished he had made the earth. Then he planted the seeds from the fruit, and they grew until there was much rattan and many trees bearing fruit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bilaan 'In the Beginning'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The four beings watched the growth for a long time and were well pleased, but finally Melu said, "Of what use is this earth and all the rattan and fruit if there are no people?" The others replied, "Let us make some people out of wax." So they took wax and worked long, fashioning it into forms; but when they brought the figures to the fire the wax melted, and they saw that men could not be made in that way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bilaan 'In the Beginning'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Next they decided to try dirt, and Melu and one of his companions began working. All went well until they were ready to make the noses: the companion, working on that part, put them on upside down. Melu told him the people would drown if he left them that way, but he refused to change them. When his back was turned, however, Melu seized the noses one by one and turned them as they now are — but he was in such a hurry that he pressed his finger at the root, and it left a mark in the soft clay which you can still see on the faces of people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bilaan 'In the Beginning'; not verbatim.

region.en: Mayo River, Davao Oriental, Mindanao, Philippines (Mandaya homeland)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨東達沃省馬耀河（曼達雅人故地）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Mandaya: 'The Children of the Limokon', eBook #12814

summary.en: In the very early days, the limokon doves were powerful and could talk like men. One limokon laid two eggs, one at the mouth of the Mayo River and one farther up its course; the first hatched a man, the second a woman. The man lived alone on the riverbank until a hair swept against his legs as he crossed the river; following the current upstream, he found the woman, and they married — their many children are the Mandaya still living along the Mayo River.
summary.zh: 太初之世，利莫康鳥神力無邊，形雖似鳥而言如人。一利莫康產二卵，一於馬耀河口，一於上游；前者孵化為男，後者為女。男子獨居河岸甚久，一日渡河時有髮絲強力沖撞其腿；溯流而上，終尋得女子，二人成婚——其眾多子孫即今居馬耀河畔之曼達雅人。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Mandaya narrators; presented as an archival record. Ethnogenesis legend: humanity born of bird eggs on the river, with the first couple united by a hair in the current.

passages.text: In the very early days, before there were any people on the earth, the limokon, a kind of dove, were very powerful and could talk like men though they looked like birds. One limokon laid two eggs, one at the mouth of the Mayo River and one farther up its course. After some time these eggs hatched, and the one at the mouth of the river became a man, while the other became a woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Children of the Limokon'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The man lived alone on the bank of the river for a long time, very lonely, and wished many times for a companion. One day when he was crossing the river something was swept against his legs with such force that it nearly caused him to drown. Examining it, he found it was a hair, and he determined to go up the river to find where it came from. He traveled up the stream, looking on both banks, until finally he found the woman, and he was very happy to think that at last he could have a companion. They were married and had many children, who are the Mandaya still living along the Mayo River.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Children of the Limokon'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun, the Moon, and the Lightning Crab (Mandaya)
title.zh: 日月與雷光巨蟹（曼達雅）

region.en: Mayo River, Davao Oriental, Mindanao, Philippines (Mandaya homeland)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨東達沃省馬耀河（曼達雅人故地）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Mandaya: 'The Sun and the Moon', eBook #12814

summary.en: The Sun and Moon are married, but the Sun is ugly and quarrelsome and chases the Moon eternally, sometimes almost catching her. Their first child, a great star like a man, is cut into small pieces by the angry Sun and scattered over the sky like a woman scatters rice — hence the many stars. Another child, a gigantic crab, causes lightning with each blink of his eyes, makes the tides from his hole in the sea's bottom, and when angry at his mother the Moon tries to swallow her — the people beat gongs and shout until he is frightened away.
summary.zh: 日月成婚，然太陽醜陋易怒，追逐月亮至今，時近時遠。長子為巨大星辰，形如人；被盛怒之太陽剁成小塊，如婦人撒米般散布天空——星辰由是繁多。另一子為巨蟹，一眨眼便生閃電，居海底巨穴而司潮汐；忤怒母親月亮時，竟欲吞之——世人愛月，見巨蟹近月便鳴鑼高呼，將其嚇退，月亮乃得保全。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Mandaya narrators; presented as an archival record. The giant crab is a cosmic sea-beast controlling tides and lightning; world-serpent tag is an interpretive mapping (vast creature underlying/threatening the cosmos). Gongs-against-the-eclipse custom is preserved.

passages.text: The Sun and the Moon were married, but the Sun was very ugly and quarrelsome. One day he became angry at the Moon and started to chase her. She ran very fast until she was some distance ahead of him, when she grew tired and he almost caught her. Ever since he has been chasing her, at times almost reaching her, and again falling far behind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Mandaya 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The first child of the Sun and Moon was a large star, and he was like a man. One time the Sun, becoming angry at the star, cut him up into small pieces and scattered him over the whole sky just as a woman scatters rice, and ever since there have been many stars. Another child of the Sun and Moon was a gigantic crab. He still lives and is so powerful that every time he opens and closes his eyes there is a flash of lightning. Most of the time the crab lives in a large hole in the bottom of the sea, and when he is there we have high tide; but when he leaves the hole, the waters rush in and there is low tide. His moving about also causes great waves on the surface of the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Mandaya 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The crab is quarrelsome like his father, and he sometimes becomes so angry with his mother, the Moon, that he tries to swallow her. When the people on earth, who are fond of the Moon, see the crab near her, they run out of doors and shout and beat on gongs until he is frightened away, and thus the Moon is saved. This is the tale of the eclipse and of the custom of driving the devourer off with gongs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Mandaya 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Widow's Son: The Seven Warriors, the Giant, and the Spirit of the Stone
title.zh: 寡婦之子：七武士、巨人與石神

region.en: Zamboanga peninsula, western Mindanao, Philippines (Subanun homeland)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨三寶顏半島（蘇巴農人故地）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Subanun: 'The Widow's Son', eBook #12814

summary.en: A widow's son kills a white-legged pig that runs seven times up the mountain before dying on a great flat rock; a door opens in the stone and he spends seven days feasting with its master, who makes a brother of him. On the way home seven color-robed warriors with matching eyes attack him, and a spirit calls his weapons from home to defend him; he slays all seven in three days' fighting, then a giant, before the spirit reveals that the stone spirit sent the seven to kill him because it saw he would marry the orphan girl it wished to wed. Wine restored the slain to life, and at the great feast the widow's son married the orphan while the stone spirit wedded another.
summary.zh: 寡婦之子獵得一頭四足皆白之豬；豬七度奔上山巔，終斃於巨岩。岩中忽開一門，主人以七彩之衣盛宴款待，結為兄弟。歸途中七位衣色各異、眼色相配之武士截殺他；家中的矛盾劍受神靈召喚而來，他血戰三日連斃七人，再戰巨人三日，殺之而焚其宅。神靈揭示：石神見他命中將娶孤女（石神所願者），遂遣七武士殺他。眾人以酒復活死者，大宴上寡婦之子娶孤女，石神另娶美人。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Subanun narrators; presented as an archival record. Heroic quest tale with fate seen in the hand, slain enemies restored by wine, and a spirit-fated marriage.

passages.text: In a little house at the edge of a village lived a widow with her only son, and they made their living growing rice in clearings on the mountainside and hunting wild pig in the forest. One evening, with their meat low, the boy asked his mother to prepare rice before daylight so he could hunt. At dawn he set out with his spear and dog, walked far into the thick forest, and rested on a rock under the hot sun, chewing betel-nut, when his dog began barking sharply. He ran toward it and saw a fine large pig, all black save its four legs which were white.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Widow's Son'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Six times the pig stopped just long enough for the boy to take aim, and then started on before he could throw, running straight up the mountain; the seventh time it halted on top of a large flat rock, and the boy succeeded in killing it. As he tied its legs, a door in the great stone swung open and a man stepped out asking why he had killed his master's pig. The boy followed him inside to a large room whose ceiling and floor were covered with cloth of seven wide red stripes alternating with seven yellow, and whose master wore trousers, jacket, and head-kerchief of seven colors. They chewed betel-nut and drank seven cups of wine from a jar so large a seat had to be brought for the boy to drink from its reed. The master did not blame him for the pig, declared he wished to make a brother of him, and the boy remained seven days in the stone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Widow's Son'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the journey home he was met by seven men, each armed with spear, shield, and sword, dressed in different colors, each man's eyes the color of his clothes. The leader in red said they were warriors who went up and down the world killing whatever they saw that had life, and now they must kill him also. A voice near him cried, "Fight, for they will try to kill you," and looking up he saw his spear, shield, and sword which he had left at home, sent by a spirit. For three days and nights they contended, and never before had the seven seen one man so brave; on the fourth day the leader fell dead, then one by one the other six. Crazed with fighting, the widow's son thought no more of home but started out to find more to slay.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Widow's Son'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He came to the home of a great giant whose house was already full of the men he had conquered, and challenged him; the giant, whose spear-shaft was the trunk of a tree, called him only a fly, but for three days and nights they struggled until the giant fell wounded at the waist. The boy burned the giant's house, and the spirit spoke again: "The seven men whom you killed were sent to kill you by the spirit of the great stone, for he looked in your hand and saw that you were to marry the orphan girl whom he himself wished to wed. But you have conquered. Go home now and prepare a great quantity of wine, for I shall bring your enemies to life again, and you will all live in peace." His mother welcomed him home as one returned from the dead; jars of wine filled the widow's house, and that night at the great feast the spirit of the great stone, his seven warriors, the friendly spirit, and the giant all came. The widow's son married the orphan girl, while another beautiful woman became the wife of the spirit of the stone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Widow's Son'; not verbatim.
